normalized.description: To develop an active antenna combined software and hardware demonstrator representative of a LEO satellite payload by exploiting advanced strategies for real time dynamically managing radio resources.Description: On-board satellite resource allocationstrategiesare essential for managing the distribution of limited resources from the antennas to multiple user terminals. These strategies involve dynamic allocation techniques that can adjust in real-time based on traffic demand. However, in dense traffic scenarios like onboard LEO satellites, these strategies face significant challenges. The high volume of demand can lead to congestion, resulting in increased latency and reduced QoS. Additionally, the limited on-board processing capability challenges the satellite's ability to efficiently manage traffic which leads to degraded antenna performance. Considering these challenges, the objective of this activity isto develop an active antenna combined software and hardware demonstrator representative of a LEO satellite payload by exploiting advanced strategies for dynamically managing radio resources, i.e. beamforming for real time tracking and coverage change combined with power and bandwidth allocation. To develop the prototypes of the most relevant solutions identified, to confirm the predicted performance. To provide road-map to flight models. The state of art TTC Sub-System architectures for Science and Exploration missions are nowadays quite complex. In order to allow communications during all mission phases, several antennas are needed in combination with redundant High Power Amplifiers (HPA) and transponders (DST). The interconnectionamong these components is accomplished by the RF Distribution Unit (RFDU), which has to guarantee the maximum degree of reconfigurability and reliability to failures. In addition, it has also to implement the necessary filtering action, to allow full duplex communications. Its design is therefore quite complex encompassing the use of several switches, Diplexers, Filters and interconnecting waveguides (WG) runs. The latter can be quite long as they have to reach antennas which are typically far from the location of the rest of the TTC subsystem. All this results in high losses with RF power reduction in transmission and increased noise figure in reception.The design solutions used so far in the frame of ESA projects are quite recurrent with no major improvements in the last decades. As shown in a TTC Sub-System architecture survey carried out in 2017, different approaches exist, as identified for example by other agencies and already flown successfully in the past years. The state of art TTC Sub-System architectures for Science and Exploration missions are nowadays quite complex. In order to allow communications during all mission phases, several antennas are needed in combination with redundant High Power Amplifiers (HPA) and transponders (DST). The interconnectionamong these components is accomplished by the RF Distribution Unit (RFDU), which has to guarantee the maximum degree of reconfigurability and reliability to failures. In addition, it has also to implement the necessary filtering action, to allow full duplex communications. Its design is therefore quite complex encompassing the use of several switches, Diplexers, Filters and interconnecting waveguides (WG) runs. The latter can be quite long as they have to reach antennas which are typically far from the location of the rest of the TTC subsystem. All this results in high losses with RF power reduction in transmission and increased noise figure in reception.The design solutions used so far in the frame of ESA projects are quite recurrent with no major improvements in the last decades. As shown in a TTC Sub-System architecture survey carried out in 2017, different approaches exist, as identified for example by other agencies and already flown successfully in the past years. For a complex RFDU as used in Deep Space missions, we can consider RF path losses in the order of 1 to 3 dB in X-band and 3 to 4 dB in Ka-band, withsignificant impacts in terms of data return (up to50% reduction) and in terms of spacecraft recovery possibilities in case of anomalies (increasedoperations complexity and limitation on maximum achievable distance). Therefore, there is a clear need for loss reduction in the RFDU paths, through the implementation of novel solutions. A study is on-going to consolidate the possible alternative subsystem Architectures, and define relevant requirements. The AOCS sensor DTs includefunctional and performance behaviour, complemented by physical behaviour (thermal, power, electronic, etc.), as well as failure and degradation modes. This detailed modelling is based on analytic and background suppliermodels. The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) combined techniques, potentiallyaugmented with analytical a priori knowledge, offer the potential to improve the overall accuracy and validity ofthis modelling, together with a specific interest for statistical interpretation in the case of mass production (sensors for constellations, for example, gyros, star trackers, sun sensors). These new engineering techniques aimed at better fidelity in the AOCS sensor modelling offer the prospect of extending the benefits to on-board performance, for example, by adapting these techniques to the ultimate AOCS sensor calibration: self-calibration on board the spacecraft (e.g. constellation or low-cost platform). The following techniques and use cases will be studied:- Digital Twin for AOCS sensors, preferably from sensors used on platform series: architecture; interoperabilityneeds, multi-physic modelling trade-off and key components; use of data-driven techniques (AI/ML) to populate the DT models; statistical interpretation and validation of AOCS sensor performance (mass manufacturing, groundself-calibration based on sample measurements and statisticextrapolation).- Use of ground models and knowledge for on-board self-calibration; data fusion techniques for on-board use to consolidate ground self-calibration with flight measurements, autonomously; autonomous verification of on-board self-calibration (fault detection).This activity will bring tools, methods, and processes for increasing the end-to-end autonomous handling of AOCS sensorsin the platform development and verification chain. It includes predictive maintenance monitoring to inform on the overall health status and to prevent anomalies/failures. This activity aims at providing digital data and models to improve knowledge of the units in flight, allowing correction and improvement by the supplier and better integration in model-based system engineering (MBSE) or digital production.This activity encompasses the following tasks:- Define the system into which the deliverable items will be integrated, establish the end user requirements andquantify the advantages of utilising the new items with respect to state-of-the-art alternatives.- Define a complete, self-standing and traceable set of technical requirements for the deliverable items.- Select the technical baseline that offers the best potential to achieve the activity objectives.- Detailed design and demonstrate, by appropriate analyses, simulations, tests or other means, that it cansatisfy the technical requirements.- Establish all detailed plans necessary to successfully implement and test the deliverable items and verify theircompliance to the technical specifications.- Implement the deliverable items, quantify their performances by means of a suitable test campaign anddemonstrate compliance to the technical requirements.

normalized.title: SECONDARY HEAT EXCHANGER FOR COMBUSTION CHAMBER COOLING OF ROCKET ENGINES - EXPRO+
normalized.description: The objective of this activity is to develop a cooling approach for steady state rocket engines to enable the use of more cost-effective materials. This should be achieved with the use of secondary heat exchange.Currently only two cooling approaches are used forrocket motor chamber design. Direct regenerative cooling with the propellants or much simpler radiative cooling. Regenerative cooling recovers energy lost in the radiative approach and offers both higher performance and, wider material options which is possible due to the lower operating temperature.Regenerative cooling is almost never limited by the sensible enthalpy, the temperature rise of the cooling propellants. It is typically limited by local effects in the cooling channel design. These effects come down to two factors the local geometry and the local vapor pressure of the coolant. The geometry is naturally constrained by the need for a rocketchamber shape.In the absence of local geometric options then the local vapor pressure can only be improved for a given propellant by driving up the local static pressure. This rules out many in-space applications where gas pressurized feed systems are the norm, the static pressure is too low. The power for high pressure pumps to regeneratively cool current spacecraft engines would require pumps more than 1.5 kWs. An alternative approach is to design a heat exchanger to transfer the heat from the wall of the combustion chamber to propellant indirectly. This has the advantage of allowing the design of specified cooling rates independent of the geometryor propellant feed conditions. Either end of the exchanger can be designed to operate at specified temperatures. This simplifies the material selection of the chamber and the transfer of energy to the propellant.A fixed temperature exchanger would have none of the limiting factors of a classical regeneratively cooled chamber. It could also simplify start up transient for many larger engine cycles. The more benign operating conditions would also allow for greater reusability; thermal gradients could be more tightly managed and more robust materials could be used, eliminating issues such as plasticity and deformations of the cooling channels. As statedearlier local conditions drive the failure in regenerative engines these are compounded when the engine flow conditions are dynamicwhen throttling. Lander engines tend to require deep throttle rates. Secondary heat exchangers operate outside these constraints and would maintain thermal integrity of deeper throttling designs. Similarly higher performance engine architectures such as aerospikes are inhibited from adoption due to the thermal complexity ofimplementing them compared to classical designs. Various ideas have been considered; however liquid metals are only one potential solution. Active pumping of a secondary coolant would also be feasible.This activity shall focus on the concept of secondary heat exchange design for high performance engine design and demonstrate a secondary heat exchanger unit by firing a representative breadboard. This would allow a greater exploitation of the propellant sensibleenthalpy than current regenerative approaches. In addition, secondary heat exchange would allow low pressure drop designs and enable actively cooled design applications where currently radiative cooling is mandated. Finally secondary heat exchange would allow theenergy to be exploited in other systems if required: repressurization, power recovery, etc. The activity encompasses the following tasks: Analysis of the state of the art of secondary heat exchanger options for combustion chamber applications. Develop and manufacture a breadboard of a secondary heat exchanger for combustion chamber. Demonstrate a secondary heat exchanger for combustion chamber design by firing a representative breadboard with heat exchanger or an appropriatesimulator. Validate the design tools toimplement such a chamber.NOTE: This activity is currently in the GSTP Work Plan but will only be implemented after confirmation offinancial support from Delegations. The final list of participating states will be known at tender issue.

Regenerative cooling recovers energy lost in the radiative approach and offers both higher performance and, wider material options which is possible due to the lower operating temperature.Regenerative cooling is almost never limited by the sensible enthalpy, the temperature rise of the cooling propellants. It is typically limited by local effects in the cooling channel design. These effects come down to two factors the local geometry and the local vapor pressure of the coolant. The geometry is naturally constrained by the need for a rocketchamber shape.In the absence of local geometric options then the local vapor pressure can only be improved for a given propellant by driving up the local static pressure. This rules out many in-space applications where gas pressurized feed systems are the norm, the static pressure is too low. The power for high pressure pumps to regeneratively cool current spacecraft engines would require pumps more than 1.5 kWs. An alternative approach is to design a heat exchanger to transfer the heat from the wall of the combustion chamber to propellant indirectly. This has the advantage of allowing the design of specified cooling rates independent of the geometryor propellant feed conditions. Either end of the exchanger can be designed to operate at specified temperatures. This simplifies the material selection of the chamber and the transfer of energy to the propellant.A fixed temperature exchanger would have none of the limiting factors of a classical regeneratively cooled chamber. It could also simplify start up transient for many larger engine cycles. The more benign operating conditions would also allow for greater reusability; thermal gradients could be more tightly managed and more robust materials could be used, eliminating issues such as plasticity and deformations of the cooling channels. As statedearlier local conditions drive the failure in regenerative engines these are compounded when the engine flow conditions are dynamicwhen throttling. Lander engines tend to require deep throttle rates. Secondary heat exchangers operate outside these constraints and would maintain thermal integrity of deeper throttling designs. Similarly higher performance engine architectures such as aerospikes are inhibited from adoption due to the thermal complexity ofimplementing them compared to classical designs. Various ideas have been considered; however liquid metals are only one potential solution. Active pumping of a secondary coolant would also be feasible.This activity shall focus on the concept of secondary heat exchange design for high performance engine design and demonstrate a secondary heat exchanger unit by firing a representative breadboard. This would allow a greater exploitation of the propellant sensibleenthalpy than current regenerative approaches. In addition, secondary heat exchange would allow low pressure drop designs and enable actively cooled design applications where currently radiative cooling is mandated. Finally secondary heat exchange would allow theenergy to be exploited in other systems if required: repressurization, power recovery, etc. The activity encompasses the following tasks: Analysis of the state of the art of secondary heat exchanger options for combustion chamber applications. Develop and manufacture a breadboard of a secondary heat exchanger for combustion chamber. Demonstrate a secondary heat exchanger for combustion chamber design by firing a representative breadboard with heat exchanger or an appropriatesimulator. Validate the design tools toimplement such a chamber.NOTE: This activity is currently in the GSTP Work Plan but will only be implemented after confirmation offinancial support from Delegations. The final list of participating states will be known at tender issue.

In previous projects (in particular, EL1-077) building blocks for this technology have been developed. The IAEA has expressed interest in a joint project to increase the protection against additional attacks identified and to raise the TRL level and to make the tracker ready forcommercialization. The objective of the activity is to study, design, implement and demonstrate a resilient and robust GNSS tracker to support IAEA safeguards activities, and other similar activities requiring Assured PNTThe tasks to be performed shall include:Based on EL1-077, the activity will study, design, implement and demonstrate the technologies required for the GNSS tracker, capable of detecting and mitigating jamming, meaconing and spoofing attacks, with focus on concrete uses cases and attack scenarios identified by IAEA.Additional technologies (for example tightly coupled INS and CRPAs) will be integrated into a functional prototype. As part of the demonstration, the prototype will be subject to thorough tests representative of challenging jamming, meaconing and spoofing scenarios mounted by capable attackers.The activity is part of a roadmap to make available to customers GNSS trackers with Assured PNT and will bring the technology to a TRL which will allow industry to make confident proposals for an Element 2. The activity will not include any Galileo PRS technology, as per NAVISP Declaration.

Furthermore, ESA's industrial partners rely onthe extensive past heritage andvalidation of these non-European solutions, and adapting a European solution would require having dataavailable so that it can be done with confidence. This activity focuses also on validating and qualifyingexisting European adhesive candidates to demonstrate their suitability for space-relevant bonding processes. Rather than developing new formulations, the goal is to rigorously benchmark available European products, perform the necessary environmental and mechanical testing, and generatea complete qualification dataset. normalized.title: VERY LARGE AND MODULAR SOLAR ARRAYS FOR IN-ORBIT ROBOTIC ASSEMBLY - EXPRO+
normalized.description: Objective: To develop and manufacture a robotic testbed to demonstrate the modular solar arrays robotic assembly, and validate the functionality in a laboratory environment, validating solar array modules design, and mechanical/electrical interfaces.Description: The activity aim is to develop a very large and modular solar array that is suitable to power very large space structures and thatcan be assembled in orbit. The design of the solar array and process of manufacturing on-ground shall be developed to target the modularity but with emphasis in covering a very large area, as well as allowing in-orbit integration. These can be achieved by exploiting existing technologies or proposing novel concepts. Concentrated Photovoltaics can be also considered, particularly for large structures targeting Deep Space missions. The assembly of solar panels within in-orbit large space structures requires careful analysisof the panels mechanical and electrical interactions and interfaces, to enable the use of robots for interlinking and assembling the necessary infrastructure. This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Definition and design of modular solar arrays and themechanical and electrical interfaces interconnecting them, suitable for building large area space structures. Targeting to obtain solar arrays 2 or 4 times bigger than current state-of-the-art. - Development and manufacturing of a robotic testbed to demonstrate the modular solar arrays robotic assembly. - Prototyping of electrical and mechanical interfaces between panels and with the robotic systems. - Initial proof of concept demonstration, verify functionality in a laboratory environment, validating solar array modules design, and mechanical/electrical interfaces.
